## What the diagram plots
The Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram plots stars by luminosity (or absolute magnitude) on the vertical axis against effective surface temperature (or spectral class, or colour) on the horizontal axis. Temperature runs backwards: hot stars, around 30,000-40,000 K, are on the left and cool stars, around 2,500 K, on the right. It goes back to work by Ejnar Hertzsprung (1911) and Henry Norris Russell (1913).
Sources: atnf-hr-intro, atnf-hr-classifying, chandra-hr

## The main groups
Most stars, including the Sun, lie on the main sequence, a band from cool, dim stars at lower right to hot, luminous stars at upper left; these stars fuse hydrogen to helium in their cores. Giants and supergiants are luminous stars that have evolved off the main sequence and lie above it. White dwarfs are hot but dim and lie at lower left; they are roughly the size of Earth. About 90 percent of stars are on the main sequence. The Sun is a G2 star with an effective temperature of about 5,800 K.
Sources: atnf-hr-intro, atnf-hr-classifying, chandra-stellar-evolution, esa-stellar-types

## Why position tells you size
The energy a star emits per unit surface area per second rises with the fourth power of its temperature (the Stefan-Boltzmann relation). Two stars with the same temperature but very different luminosities must therefore differ in size: the more luminous one has the larger surface. That is why a cool but very luminous star must be a giant, and a hot but dim one must be a white dwarf.
Sources: atnf-hr-intro, chandra-hr

## Luminosity classes
Stars of one spectral type are further divided by luminosity class: I and II supergiants and bright giants, III giants, IV subgiants, V main-sequence stars, VI subdwarfs and VII white dwarfs.
Sources: chandra-hr

## What is needed to place an object
Placing an object on the H-R diagram needs two quantities: its effective temperature (or spectral type or colour) and its luminosity (or absolute magnitude). Absolute magnitude is the brightness the star would have at 10 parsecs, so it requires knowing the distance. A SPHEREx Spectral Image gives a surface brightness at one wavelength; by itself it gives neither temperature nor luminosity. If either quantity is missing, Q-FIT says which one and does not assign a position.
Sources: atnf-hr-classifying, spherex-data-products, qfit-spec

## Mass and the main sequence
On the main sequence a star's properties are set almost entirely by its mass. More massive stars are more luminous, with luminosity rising roughly as the fourth power of mass, and they spend less time on the main sequence. There is no such mass-luminosity relation for giants or white dwarfs.
Sources: chandra-stellar-evolution
